evidence.claim: Route 62 leaves Interstate 10 at the eastern end of San Gorgonio Pass and heads north toward Morongo Valley.
evidence.quote: It begins at a freeway-to-freeway interchange with Interstate 10 at the eastern end of the San Gorgonio Pass northwest of Palm Springs in Riverside County. It heads due north until its intersection with SR 247 in Yucca Valley

evidence.claim: The highway crosses the Little San Bernardino Mountains, but its recognized scenic stretch covers just nine miles, from I-10 to the Riverside–San Bernardino county line.
evidence.quote: SR 62 cuts across the Little San Bernardino Mountains along southern San Bernardino County.

evidence.claim: The road acquired its state identity in pieces. White Water to Morongo Valley entered the state system in 1935; the continuation to Yucca Valley followed in 1959. Both belonged to Route 187.
evidence.quote: The routing west of Twentynine Palms was added to the state highway system in phases, with the part from White Water to Morongo Valley added in 1935, and from Morongo Valley to Yucca Valley in 1959; both were designated as Route 187.

evidence.claim: The 1964 renumbering brought the route from I-10 to Twentynine Palms under the SR 62 number. Its extension to Arizona followed in 1970.
evidence.quote: In the 1964 state highway renumbering, SR 62 was designated from I-10 into the town of Twentynine Palms. The portion from Twentynine Palms to Arizona was added to SR 62 in 1970.

evidence.claim: Beyond the designated section, Morongo Valley provides the entrance to Big Morongo Canyon Preserve, just off Route 62.
evidence.quote: The entrance to the preserve is located within Morongo Valley, California, an unincorporated place within San Bernardino County just off California State Route 62.

evidence.claim: There, mountain drainage and the Morongo fault create a creek and marsh in the desert.
evidence.quote: The Morongo fault running through the canyon causes water draining from the surrounding mountains to form Big Morongo Creek and the marsh habitat.

evidence.claim: Wind development at San Gorgonio Pass began in the 1980s, but an earlier experiment used a salvaged roller-coaster generator.
evidence.quote: Development of the wind farm began in the 1980s.

evidence.claim: In 1926, Dew R. Oliver and electrician W. Sperry Knighton built a turbine near Whitewater. They fitted the generator with aluminum propellers and a funnel to concentrate the wind, then mounted it on a circular rail so it could turn.
evidence.quote: In 1926 Oliver, in collaboration with electrician W. Sperry Knighton, built a wind turbine near Whitewater. The original device used a generator Oliver had salvaged from an old roller coaster at Seal Beach, California. Oliver and Sperry fitted the generator with aluminum propellers, and placed a large funnel on the front to concentrate the wind's power. They set the entire device on a circular rail that allowed it to be pivoted to face prevailing winds.

evidence.claim: That machine was dismantled for scrap in 1942. More recent repowering replaces groups of small, aging turbines with fewer, larger machines.
evidence.quote: The device he had built near Whitewater became a landmark and curiosity until it was taken down and sold for scrap in 1942.

evidence.claim: More recent repowering replaces groups of small, aging turbines with fewer, larger machines.
evidence.quote: The reduction is the result of repowering, where many small, obsolete turbines are replaced with fewer, larger turbines.

evidence.claim: Stone cabins and a small swimming pool once served an early twentieth-century guest ranch at Mission Creek. Remnants remain visible near the entrance.
evidence.quote: In the early 20th century the site hosted a guest ranch, with stone cabins and a small swimming pool; remnants are still visible near the entrance.

evidence.claim: The Wildlands Conservancy acquired the property in 1997 and opened it for low-impact recreation; it became part of Sand to Snow National Monument in 2016.
evidence.quote: In 1997, The Wildlands Conservancy acquired the property and opened it for low-impact public recreation. The area was included within Sand to Snow National Monument upon its designation in 2016.

evidence.claim: The preserve occupies the transition between the Mojave and Sonoran deserts. At Painted Hills Wetland, cottonwoods and other streamside vegetation mark a different habitat from the adjacent mountain slopes and desert washes.
evidence.quote: Mission Creek Preserve sits in a transition zone between the Mojave Desert and Sonoran Desert, resulting in flora and fauna from both deserts. Painted Hills Wetland, shown on preserve maps, is a broad wetland area that supports cottonwoods and other riparian vegetation;

evidence.claim: adjacent mountain slopes and desert washes.
evidence.quote: Habitats include riparian zones, desert washes, and adjacent mountain slopes.

evidence.claim: Water gives Big Morongo Canyon its marsh. The Morongo fault causes drainage from the surrounding mountains to form Big Morongo Creek and the marsh habitat.
evidence.quote: The Morongo fault running through the canyon causes water draining from the surrounding mountains to form Big Morongo Creek and the marsh habitat.

evidence.claim: The canyon begins in the Mojave Desert and opens downstream into the Colorado Desert.
evidence.quote: The upstream end of the canyon originates in the Mojave Desert, while its downstream portion opens into the Colorado Desert.

evidence.claim: A spring-fed oasis supports cottonwoods and willows.
evidence.quote: The natural spring fed desert oasis found here is one of the 10 largest Cottonwood (Populus fremontii) and Willow (Salix lasiolepis) riparian habitats in California.

evidence.claim: Lands contributed and managed by the Nature Conservancy, San Bernardino County and the Bureau of Land Management formed the preserve in 1982.
evidence.quote: The Nature Conservancy, San Bernardino County, and the United States Bureau of Land Management all contributed and managed the lands which were organized to create the preserve in 1982.

evidence.claim: The Marsh and Mesquite trails are each under a mile, giving this excursion from Morongo Valley a smaller scale than the longer canyon route.
evidence.quote: The preserve has several short trails, such as the Marsh and Mesquite trails which are under a mile long, while the Canyon trail is approximately 10 miles (16 km) round-trip.

evidence.claim: At the pass, mountains flank a transition from the Mediterranean climate to the west to desert climate on the east.
evidence.quote: Flanked by Mount San Gorgonio and the Transverse Ranges to the North, and Mount San Jacinto and the Peninsular Ranges to the South, the San Gorgonio Pass is a transitional zone from a Mediterranean climate west of the pass, to a Desert climate east of the pass.

evidence.claim: In 1961, the state added Yucca Valley to Twentynine Palms as Route 218, another piece of the future highway.
evidence.quote: From Yucca Valley to Twentynine Palms, Route 218 was added in 1961.

evidence.claim: Southern California Edison began testing two turbine generators near its Devers substation in 1980.
evidence.quote: Southern California Edison opened its Wind Energy Center eight miles northwest of Palm Springs in 1980 near its Devers substation, installing two wind turbine generators for testing.
